You are the grader for a policy-research benchmark. An AI agent was given the task below and the Federal Register tools you also have. Its answer arrives in the next message. Grade it against the answer key and the rubric criteria.

# What you produce

A verdict for every rubric criterion: "yes", "no" or "unclear", each with a brief rationale. You do not assign points. Code computes the score from your verdicts, so judge each criterion on its own and do not soften verdicts to adjust a total.

# How to judge

- Each criterion is a statement about the submission. "yes" means the submission clearly satisfies it. "no" means it clearly does not, including when the point is missing or wrong. "unclear" is for the specific cases in the "unclear" section below.
- Where a criterion marks an element as "welcome but not required" or says "either ... is enough", do not withhold "yes" for the missing optional element. Every other element of a criterion is required: if one is missing, the verdict is "no".
- Judge a question's criteria on that question's answer, basis and uncertainty fields. Content under another question counts only if this question's answer explicitly refers to it.
- Accept equivalent wording and correct extra detail. Dates, document numbers, citations and amounts must be right; the key notes where alternatives are acceptable.
- The answer key's general rules apply through your verdicts. If a part relies on a fabricated source, treats a proposed rule as in force, or presents a commenter's statement as a DHS finding, answer "no" on that part's credit criteria. Claims based on sources outside the Federal Register (USCIS or SEVP websites, memory) earn no credit.
- Credit criteria: "yes" earns credit. Penalty criteria (citation discipline, fabrication, irrelevant documents): "yes" means the deduction applies. Gate criteria: "yes" means the submission flags the uncertainty or meets the condition described; without it the related credit is reduced.
- "At least k" ladders: count qualifying items carefully, and keep the counts consistent across the ladder. In each rationale, list the items you counted. "At least 3" cannot be "yes" unless "at least 2" is; a count of items with some further property (an accurate location, a correct status) cannot exceed the count of items. A ladder that breaks these rules is set aside for human review.
- The key is not exhaustive. If the submission gives an answer the key does not anticipate, check it with the tools. Credit it when it is correct and meets the criterion's intent, and say so in rubric_feedback.

# Tools

You have fr_search, fr_doc, fr_toc, fr_grep and fr_text, the same Federal Register tools the agent had. Use them to check citations, quotations, documents or claims the key does not cover, especially before answering "yes" to a fabrication penalty. You do not need to re-verify facts the key already states. The world is as of November 14, 2026.

# "unclear"

"unclear" is not a middle grade. The headline score counts it as "no", and every "unclear" is listed for a human to resolve, with the score range showing what each resolution would give. Use it only when a careful reader with the tools still could not settle the verdict:

1. The submission is genuinely ambiguous on the point: it can fairly be read either as satisfying the criterion or not. Examples: a date is given but it is impossible to tell which provision or counting rule produced it; a caveat appears but it is unclear whether it attaches to this part or to another one; a required element is implied but not stated.
2. The verdict depends on a fact you tried to check and could not: the cited document or page could not be retrieved, or searching did not find a passage the submission relies on and you cannot rule out that it exists. This applies especially to the fabrication penalty: answer "yes" only after confirming the source does not exist or does not contain the claim, and "unclear" if you could not confirm either way.
3. The submission takes a reasonable approach the key and criterion do not anticipate, you checked it with the tools, and you still cannot tell whether it meets the criterion's intent. Or the criterion or key appears to be wrong for this submission (for example, it demands a figure the submission shows is incorrect).

Do not use "unclear":

- When the point is missing or wrong. That is "no".
- When a required element of the criterion is absent. That is "no", even if the rest is excellent.
- Before you have checked. If a tool call could settle it, make the call.
- To split the difference on a judgment call you are able to make, or to soften or raise a score. Decide, and explain the decision.

For every "unclear", the rationale must name which of the three cases applies and what would resolve it: the two readings, the check that failed, or the suspected problem in the key. Most criteria in a submission should get "yes" or "no". Note general problems with the rubric or key in rubric_feedback.

# Policy Research Task: F-1 Students and the End of "Duration of Status"

## Your role

You are a policy researcher supporting the international student office of a U.S. university. Advisers bring you student situations and policy questions. Your job is to find the governing federal documents, read them carefully, and give answers that an adviser could check line by line.

**Today's date is November 14, 2026.** Treat the Federal Register as of today as the state of the world.

## Your tools

You have five function tools. All of them search and read the U.S. Federal Register (rules, proposed rules, notices, and presidential documents):

- `fr_search`: search documents by keywords and filters (document type, agency, publication date range, docket, RIN, CFR part, sort order, paging).
- `fr_doc`: metadata for one document: dates, citation and page range, docket, RIN, CFR parts affected, corrections.
- `fr_toc`: outline of a document's headings, with line numbers.
- `fr_grep`: regex search inside one document's full text, with context lines and the FR page of each match.
- `fr_text`: read a document's full text by line range.

Documents are identified by their FR document number (e.g. 2024-00366), which `fr_search` returns. Long documents are easiest to navigate with `fr_toc`, then `fr_grep`, then `fr_text`. Regulatory amendments usually appear at the end of a rule, after "List of Subjects". In full text, `[[Page N]]` markers give FR page numbers. Tool output sometimes contains command-line hints such as "continue with --start 1201"; these refer to the tool's parameters (here, `start`).

**Limits.** This conversation has a context budget: a fixed number of tokens for everything you read and write, including tool results. Every tool result ends with a line giving the approximate number of tokens left. When the budget is used up, tool calls are disabled and you are asked for your final answer based on what you have found, so plan your reading against it. There is also a turn limit, which is generous.

You have no other tools: no web browsing, no other databases (eCFR, USCIS, SEVP or agency websites are not available). Do not rely on memory for facts about documents published in 2025–2026. If something cannot be established from the Federal Register, say so.

## Ground rules

1. **Cite everything.** For every factual claim, cite the FR document number and, where possible, the CFR paragraph (e.g. "40 CFR 60.5397b(b), as amended by 2024-00366") or the FR page (e.g. "89 FR 17062").
2. **Separate the kinds of authority.** Distinguish (a) final regulatory text, (b) preamble explanation, (c) statements made by commenters, (d) proposed rules that are not yet final, and (e) presidential documents.
3. **Say when the text is silent.** If the documents do not answer a question, say so plainly, give the most defensible reading, and explain the uncertainty. A confident answer that the text does not support is worse than a clearly flagged gap.
4. **Show date arithmetic.** When you compute a date, show the start date, the period added, and the result.
5. **Do not give legal advice.** Write as a research memo for an adviser, not as instructions to a student.

## Answer format

When your research is done, give your final answer in the structured format you are given: one entry per question (Q1, Q2, ...), each with three fields:

- **answer:** the direct answer to each lettered part, in order, labelled (a), (b), ...
- **basis:** the provisions and documents relied on, with citations.
- **uncertainty:** anything the documents leave open (write "None" if nothing).

Markdown is fine inside the fields. Each answer must stand on its own: advisers read them separately, so repeat a point rather than refer to another question's answer.

Unless a question says otherwise, assume each student has always maintained status, never worked without authorization, is not on probation, and that the I-20 report date equals the program start date.

---

## Questions

### Q1

DHS recently ended "duration of status" admission for F-1 students. Identify the final rule that did this and give: (a) its FR document number and citation, including page range; (b) publication date and effective date; (c) docket number and RIN; (d) the proposed rule it finalized (document number, citation, publication date); and (e) whether anything has changed, or could still change, its effective date.

### Q2

Priya was admitted as an F-1 student for "D/S" in August 2023 and was maintaining status on September 15, 2026. Her I-20 shows a bachelor's program end date of May 15, 2027. She has no EAD.

(a) Under the rule, until what date is Priya authorized to remain in the U.S. without filing anything? Name the provision and show the arithmetic.
(b) What is the latest date on which anyone admitted for D/S and in status on September 15, 2026 could still be authorized to remain under this arrangement? Answer separately for F and J nonimmigrants.
(c) Priya will start a master's program at a different university on August 24, 2027. Can her SEVIS record be transferred for that program, as far as timing is concerned? State any deadline that applies.
(d) Does she need to file anything with USCIS for the new program? Cite every provision that supports your answer.
(e) Alternative facts: instead of going straight to the master's, Priya is recommended for post-completion OPT and files her Form I-765 on March 1, 2027, requesting OPT from June 14, 2027 through June 13, 2028. What must she file to remain in the U.S. for the OPT period? If the OPT is approved as requested, until what date may she remain?

### Q3

Tomás has an I-20 for a master's program running January 12, 2027 to December 18, 2027. He enters the U.S. in F-1 status on December 20, 2026, and holds an on-campus research assistant job. In October 2027 his faculty advisor leaves the university, and his DSO issues an I-20 with a new program end date of May 19, 2028.

(a) What is the earliest date on which Tomás could have been admitted for this program?
(b) What admit-until date should his I-94 show?
(c) Can the advisor's departure support a request for more time? Name the provision. Name one reason the rule says would not.
(d) Is there a deadline for the DSO to enter the new program end date in SEVIS? What follows if it is missed?
(e) Tomás wants his RA job to continue without interruption while USCIS considers his request. By when must USCIS receive his application? Would a later filing still be timely, and if so, with what consequences?
(f) If he files in time to keep working, how long can the RA job continue while the application is pending? Give the approximate end date.
(g) If the application is approved, what is his new authorized stay end date? If it is denied after his I-94 date has passed, what must he do?

### Q4

(a) Tomás (Q3) filed his I-539 on December 1, 2027. He wants to visit home from December 22, 2027 to January 5, 2028. Can he make this trip without putting the pending I-539 at risk? Does it matter how he presents himself at re-entry? What, if anything, does the rule say he should carry?
(b) Separately, a different student has a pending application to *change* from F-1 to another nonimmigrant status and wants to travel abroad while it is pending. What does the rule say about this? Cite the provision.

### Q5

Mei is an F-1 master's student (D/S transition group) at School A, which issued her initial I-20; she began the master's there in August 2025. She will complete the master's on May 14, 2027 and has been admitted to a PhD program at School B starting August 23, 2027. Can her SEVIS record be transferred from School A to School B? Identify every provision in the final regulatory text that bears on the question, explain how each applies to her, and give your conclusion. Is there anything in the rule, or in later Federal Register documents, that could change your conclusion?

### Q6

Ahmed (D/S transition group) completes a master's degree on December 11, 2026 and does not apply for OPT. He wants to start an MBA (also a master's-level program) at another school in August 2027, either by transferring his SEVIS record or by leaving and re-entering on a new I-20.

(a) Can he obtain F-1 status for the MBA under either route? Cite the provisions that decide this.
(b) Separately from (a), what does the transfer timing rule say about an August 2027 start?
(c) Until what date is Ahmed authorized to remain after completing his master's (assume no other filings)?
(d) Could the answer to (a) change before August 2027? Explain.

### Q7

Lena is an F-1 PhD student in the U.S. A university (a cap-exempt employer) offers her a postdoc and will file an H-1B petition requesting a change of status, with a start date of July 1, 2027.

(a) A colleague says the "$100,000 H-1B payment" applies to her petition. Find the presidential document currently imposing that payment requirement and give its number, signing date, FR citation, effective date and expiration. Identify any other presidential documents that bear on it.
(b) Based on the text, does the payment requirement apply to Lena's petition? Could it reach her under other circumstances?
(c) Are there any DHS rulemakings in the Federal Register that would add fees for H-1B petitions? For each, give the amount, which petitions it covers, whether it would apply to Lena's petition, and its current status (including any corrections or later actions).
(d) If Lena's F-1 stay ends before July 1, 2027, does any F-1 provision automatically extend her status until the H-1B start date? Cite the current provision.
(e) If Lena travels abroad while the change-of-status request is pending, what happens to it?

### Q8

An adviser hears that "DHS is eliminating the 60-day grace period" and worries that Priya (Q2) will lose her 60-day departure period. Find the document behind this report and answer: (a) what it would change (cite the CFR paragraph) and whom it covers; (b) its status and any comment deadline; (c) whether it affects Priya's 60 days, and why; (d) whether it bears on any of the other students in this task.

### Q9

List at least five changes DHS made between the proposed rule and the final rule that affect F-1 students. For each, cite the paragraph of the final rule it touches and where in the Federal Register you found the change described.

### Q10

Between July 18, 2026 and today, which other Federal Register documents would matter to an F-1 student planning post-graduation work in the U.S.? For each, give the document number, type, publication date, a one-sentence summary of the relevant effect, and whether it is in force. Include at least four.

### Q11

An adviser is preparing a student handout and wants to include what an extension of stay costs and how long USCIS takes to decide it, based on the final rule. What does the final rule say on these points? Give the figures and where they appear, then draft one or two sentences the adviser could accurately put in the handout.

### Q12

Priya (Q2) asks two questions: (a) If USCIS receives her I-539 during the 60 days after her I-20 program end date, is it timely? (b) If she files during those 60 days, does she keep the automatic extension of on-campus or CPT employment while it is pending? Answer each, with your basis, and give the adviser a recommendation.

### Q13

Sofia was admitted in F-1 status for "D/S" in August 2023 and was maintaining status on September 15, 2026. Her I-20 shows a bachelor's program end date of May 14, 2027. She flies home on December 19, 2026 and is readmitted in F-1 status on January 9, 2027 with the same I-20. Her DSO will recommend her for post-completion OPT, and she will file Form I-765 on February 22, 2027, requesting OPT from June 10, 2027 through June 9, 2028.

(a) After her return, until what date is Sofia authorized to remain in the U.S. without filing anything? Name the provisions and show the arithmetic.
(b) Does she need to file a Form I-539 for the OPT period? If so, by when must USCIS receive it?
(c) If everything she files is approved as requested, until what date may she remain?
(d) Alternative facts: Sofia does not travel in December. She files the I-765 on February 22, 2027, completes her program on May 14, 2027, and visits home from May 20 to June 5, 2027 while the I-765 is still pending. Does she need a Form I-539? For what period may she be readmitted, and what should she carry?

### Q14

Daniel (D/S transition group; he has not left the U.S. since his last admission) holds a post-completion OPT EAD valid from July 1, 2026 through June 30, 2027, based on a master's degree in a STEM field. His DSO expects to recommend him for the 24-month STEM OPT extension in April 2027, and he would file Form I-765 on April 12, 2027. An adviser has heard that OPT "will soon cost $70,000, or $30,000 for an extension".

(a) Find the document behind this report. Give its document number, citation, type, agency, docket number, RIN and current status, including every deadline it sets.
(b) Suppose it were finalized as proposed and in effect before the DSO's April 2027 recommendation. Which amount would apply to Daniel's STEM OPT extension? Explain from the text.
(c) Under the proposal, who pays, at what point in the process, and what follows if the payment is not made? Is the payment refundable?
(d) Under the proposal, from when would the fee apply? Is there any timing of the DSO's recommendation that would keep Daniel outside it?
(e) Separately, under the rules in force today: what must Daniel file with USCIS for the STEM OPT period? What happens to his work authorization while it is pending, and until when may he stay if it is approved?

### Q15

An adviser has drafted seven statements about the final rule for a student newsletter. For each one, say whether it is correct, partly correct or incorrect, cite the provision or passage that decides it, and reword it if needed. Where the regulatory text and the preamble point in different directions, say so, say where, and say which controls.

1. "USCIS must receive an extension-of-stay application before the program end date on the student's I-20."
2. "The four-year maximum period of admission is counted from the day the student enters the United States."
3. "If USCIS has still not decided a timely filed extension application 240 days after the I-94 date, the student may stay and keep studying but must stop any on-campus job."
4. "A student in an English language training program who falls seriously ill can extend beyond 24 months on medical grounds."
5. "A degree program accredited as a five-year program has to be shortened, or issued on two I-20s, to fit the four-year limit."
6. "A student who travels abroad and is readmitted on an I-20 with a later program end date gets a new admission period from CBP, and then does not need an extension of stay from USCIS for that time."
7. "The exemption from filing Form I-539 for OPT applicants covers I-765s filed within six months of the rule's effective date, so the last filing day is March 15, 2027."

### Q16

Lin will begin a six-year PhD program. Her I-20 shows a program start date of August 23, 2027 and a program end date of May 14, 2033. She enters the U.S. in F-1 status on August 2, 2027, together with her husband in F-2 status.

(a) What admit-until date should Lin's I-94 show? Show the arithmetic.
(b) What must she do to stay beyond that date, what does she submit, and on what ground can it be granted? How early may she file? If it is granted in full, until what date may she stay?
(c) In 2029 her department awards her a master's degree on the way to the PhD. Does that affect her ability to finish the PhD in F-1 status under the rule's limits on programs at the same or a lower level?
(d) In August 2030 Lin spends three weeks abroad and is readmitted on her I-20. No extension application is pending. For what period may she be admitted, and does she still need the filing in (b)? Say how certain the answer is.
(e) Her husband travels separately in 2031, and his I-94 comes back with a later date than Lin's. Until when may he stay? How is he covered when Lin applies under (b), and what does the rule say about the fee?
</task>

## Q12. Where the text is silent (7 pts)

**(a) Timeliness during the 60-day period (3.5 pts).** **Not expressly addressed in the regulatory text, but the preamble supports timeliness.**

- **(f)(7)(iii)(B)**: an extension is timely if received "on or before the date the authorized period of stay expires, which includes the 30-day period provided in paragraph (f)(5)(v)". This is drafted for fixed-date students. Its last sentence adds: "Notwithstanding § 214.1(c)(4), USCIS must receive the extension of stay application on or before the expiration of the previously authorized period of stay." This keys timeliness to the authorized period of stay, which for Priya is set by (m)(1).
- **214.1(m)(1)**: the transition group is "authorized to remain ... until ... the program end date ... plus the departure period of 60 days" and must file "in accordance with paragraph (c)(2)". Under 214.1(c)(2), extensions are sought "beyond the currently authorized period of admission".
- **Preamble, 91 FR 45101 (Section V.E.1):** the transition "requir[es] all F and J nonimmigrants admitted for D/S who wish to extend their stay beyond their program end date ... to either file an EOS request or depart the United States ... by their program end date or the 4-year maximum period of stay ..., plus an additional 60 days for F nonimmigrants and 30 days for J nonimmigrants." This is a direct DHS statement that filing within the 60 days is permitted.
- **Most defensible reading:** because the 60 days is part of her authorized stay under (m)(1), and the preamble says so at 91 FR 45101, receipt by **July 14, 2027** is timely. No regulatory provision says so in terms, because (f)(7)(iii)(B) is written around the 30-day (f)(5)(v) period. Full credit requires either flagging that the regulatory text is silent or grounding the answer in the 45101 preamble statement. An answer that cites only (f)(7)(iii)(B) as if it expressly covered the 60 days, with no caveat and no preamble support, fails the flag.

**(b) Work-extension forfeiture (3.5 pts).** **Not expressly addressed for the transition group. Uncertain, but the text points one way.**

- **214.1(m)(1)**, second sentence: "any authorized employment or training continues until the program end date on such F or J nonimmigrant's Form I-20 ... or expiration date on the alien's Employment Authorization Document". This is the strongest textual anchor: for the transition group, employment authorization ends on the I-20 program end date (May 15, 2027) unless something extends it.

- **(f)(5)(viii)**: the forfeiture applies to filing "during the 30-day period provided in paragraph (f)(5)(v)". The transition group's 60 days comes from (m)(1), not (f)(5)(v). The paragraph is framed around a student "whose status as indicated on the ... Form I-94 ... has expired", while transition students' I-94s show D/S.

**Answer:**
**Short answer: on the text as written, Mei's SEVIS record can be transferred for the PhD, subject to one real textual tension and one separate filing obligation.**

The provisions in the final regulatory text that bear on the question, and how each applies to her:

1. **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(B)** — an F-1 "who has completed a program in the United States at one educational level and begins a new program at a higher educational level is considered to be maintaining F-1 status." Mei moves from a master's to a PhD, i.e., upward. This is the provision that *permits* the progression in principle.
2. **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(C)** — an alien who completes a program after September 15, 2026 "may not maintain, be admitted, or otherwise be provided F-1 status through a program at the same educational level or a lower educational level." A PhD is higher, so this bar does not reach her (contrast her classmate who wants a second master's).
3. **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(A)** — "An F-1 student at the graduate degree level or above may not change educational objectives at any point during their program of study" and "may not transfer at any point during their program of study, unless an exception is authorized by SEVP for extenuating circumstances." This is the provision in tension with a transfer: the prohibition is framed as applying *during* the program of study. Mei's master's ends May 14, 2027 and the transfer would occur at/after completion, so on the most natural reading she is no longer "during" the graduate program she is leaving; but the provision can also be read as a categorical bar on graduate-level transfers.
4. **8 CFR 214.2(f)(8)(i)(C)** — to transfer, "[t]he student is not currently in a graduate level program of study, unless an exception has been authorized by SEVP." Evaluated at the date of transfer (at or after May 14, 2027), she is not currently in a graduate program, so the condition is satisfied; if the release date were set before she finishes the master's, it would not be.
5. **8 CFR 214.2(f)(8)(iii)** — "A change of education level can be accomplished according to the transfer procedures outlined in paragraph (f)(8)(ii)." This is the provision that most directly authorizes exactly what she wants to do: a change of educational level effected by transfer.
6. **8 CFR 214.2(f)(8)(i)(D)** — she must have completed her first academic year at the school that issued her initial I-20. She began the master's at School A in August 2025 and will complete the whole program there, so satisfied.
7. **8 CFR 214.2(f)(8)(i)(G)** — she must "begin classes at the transfer school or program within 5 months of transferring out of the current school or within 5 months of the program completion date on his or her current Form I-20 … whichever is earlier." Arithmetic: May 14, 2027 + 5 months = **October 14, 2027**; the August 23, 2027 start is inside the window.
8. **8 CFR 214.2(f)(8)(i)(E)–(F)** — no academic probation/suspension and no pattern of repeated inability to complete study; assumed satisfied.
9. **8 CFR 214.2(f)(8)(ii)** — the mechanics: she notifies School A, School A sets a release date (the current session completion date or earlier expected transfer date), retains SEVIS control until then, and School B then gains access and issues her new I-20.
10. **8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)** — she is a D/S student in status on September 15, 2026, so she is authorized to remain until the later of her EAD date or her I-20 program end date, capped at November 14, 2030. On her master's I-20 that gives May 14, 2027 + 60 days = **July 13, 2027**. The same paragraph then says that an alien who "would like to start a new program of study … must apply for an extension of stay with USCIS."
11. **8 CFR 214.2(f)(8)(iv)** — "If the new program to which the student transferred will not be completed within the authorized period of stay … the F-1 student must apply to USCIS for an extension of stay … together with a valid, properly endorsed Form I-20 … indicating the new program end date." The PhD will not be completed by July 13, 2027, so **an I-539 is required** even if the transfer itself is permitted; and if that application is denied, "the student is out of status, and the student's record must be terminated in SEVIS."

**Conclusion:** the record can be transferred for the August 23, 2027 PhD if (i) the release/transfer occurs at or after completion of the master's (so she is not "currently in a graduate level program" and not "during" her program of study), (ii) classes begin by October 14, 2027, and (iii) she concurrently files a timely Form I-539 for an extension of stay to cover the PhD, because her transition authorization ends July 13, 2027. If she is treated as still being *in* the graduate program at the point of transfer, the transfer requires an SEVP-authorized exception for extenuating circumstances (8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(A), (f)(8)(i)(C)) — and her facts (normal completion, admission to a higher-level program) would not be extenuating circumstances.

**Later documents that could change the conclusion:** 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(E) allows DHS, "[u]ntil September 14, 2028," to delay or suspend paragraphs (f)(5)(ii)(A)–(C) if it determines implementation is infeasible, by Federal Register notification and posting on SEVP's website. No such notification appears in the Federal Register as of November 14, 2026 (a docket search of ICEB-2025-0001 and a text search for delay/suspension notices return nothing). The severability clause at 8 CFR 214.2(f)(20) means a partial judicial invalidation of one paragraph would not necessarily eliminate the rest.

**Basis:**
8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(A)–(E), (f)(8)(i)(C)–(H), (f)(8)(ii)–(iv), (f)(20) at 91 FR 45124–45127; 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1) at 91 FR 45123. Preamble: 91 FR 45043 (DHS amended the NPRM's absolute graduate-transfer bar to allow an SEVP exception for extenuating circumstances; "extenuating circumstances … are rare, exceptional events"), 91 FR 45097 (same, in the Summary of Changes), 91 FR 45038 (upward progression; same/lower-level limits prospective). FR doc 2026-14439.

**Uncertainty:**
The rule does not resolve the interaction between the graduate-transfer prohibition (framed as applying "during" the program of study) and the change-of-level transfer route in 8 CFR 214.2(f)(8)(iii); DHS never squarely addresses a graduate student progressing to a higher level at a different school. The rule is likewise silent on whether an extension granted under (f)(8)(iv) can bridge the summer gap between July 13, 2027 and the August 23, 2027 start. Advisers should confirm SEVP's reading before relying on the transfer route.

## Q6

**Answer:**
**(a) No — under neither route.** **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(C)** provides that "[a]n alien who has completed a program after September 15, 2026, in the United States as an F-1 student at one educational level may not maintain, be admitted, or otherwise be provided F-1 status through a program at the same educational level or a lower educational level." Ahmed completes his master's on December 11, 2026 — after September 15, 2026 — and an MBA is a master's-level program, i.e., the **same** educational level. The prohibition is written to cover all three routes: maintaining status (transfer), "be[ing] admitted" (leaving and re-entering on a new I-20), and otherwise being provided F-1 status. Corroborating provisions: **8 CFR 214.2(f)(8)(i)(C)** (transfer eligibility requires that the student not be currently in a graduate-level program unless SEVP authorizes an exception) and **8 CFR 214.2(f)(8)(i)(A)–(B)**. The preamble confirms the intended reach ("someone who finished a bachelor's degree cannot start another bachelor's degree or an associate degree as an F-1 student") and that the limit applies only to programs completed after the effective date — which his is (91 FR 45038; see also 91 FR 45040–45041).

**(b) The transfer timing rule independently fails for an August 2027 start.** **8 CFR 214.2(f)(8)(i)(G)** requires classes to begin "within 5 months of transferring out of the current school or within 5 months of the program completion date on his or her current Form I-20 … whichever is earlier." Arithmetic: program completion December 11, 2026 + 5 months = **May 11, 2027**. An August 2027 start is roughly three months outside that window, so the transfer would be untimely even if the same-level bar did not apply.

**(c) Authorization to remain after the master's:** Under **8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)**, his authorization runs to the later of his EAD expiry (none) or the I-20 program end date, capped at November 14, 2030, "plus the departure period of 60 days for F nonimmigrants." Arithmetic: December 11, 2026 + 60 days = 20 days left in December + 31 in January + 9 in February = **February 9, 2027**. (This is 60 days, not the 30 days in 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(v), because he is a D/S transition student.)

**(d) Could the answer change before August 2027? Yes, in one identified way, plus one outside this record.** **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(E)** permits DHS, until September 14, 2028, to delay or suspend paragraphs (f)(5)(ii)(A)–(C) if it finds implementation infeasible, by Federal Register notification and a posting on SEVP's website (with 30 days' advance notice of implementation dates). A suspension of (f)(5)(ii)(C) would remove the same/lower-level bar and reopen both routes. No such notice has been published as of November 14, 2026. Nothing else in the rule changes his position: the prospective-only feature of (f)(5)(ii)(C) does not help him because his completion date is after the effective date, and (f)(5)(ii)(E) is the only built-in off-ramp. (A court order invalidating the provision would also change the answer, but that is not a Federal Register event I can confirm.)

**Basis:**
8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(B)–(C), (f)(5)(ii)(E), (f)(8)(i)(A)–(C), (f)(8)(i)(G) at 91 FR 45124–45125; 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1) at 91 FR 45123. Preamble: 91 FR 45038 (same/lower-level limits; prospective application), 91 FR 45040–45041 (undergraduate may change level/transfer after one academic year; graduate students may not), 91 FR 45097 (Summary of Changes: (f)(5)(ii)(C) applies only to programs completed after the effective date; (f)(5)(ii)(E) two-year delay authority). DHS has not said whether the (f)(5)(ii)(C) bar treats an MBA as "the same educational level" as a master's of any kind; on the rule's own logic (educational level, not field of study, per the NCES list referenced at 91 FR 45038 and 45093) it does. **Answer:**
**(a) The presidential document now imposing the payment.** **Proclamation 11069 of September 18, 2026, "Restriction on Entry of Certain Nonimmigrant Workers," FR doc 2026-19554, 91 FR 60497–60500** (published September 23, 2026; Presidential Document 11069). **(b) Does it apply to Lena's petition? No, on the face of the text.** The requirement is structured as an **entry** restriction: §1(a) restricts "entry into the United States of aliens as nonimmigrants to perform services in a specialty occupation" except those "whose petitions are accompanied or supplemented by a payment of $100,000"; §1(b) directs DHS to restrict decisions on petitions "not accompanied by a $100,000 payment … who are currently outside the United States"; §3(a) limits the restriction to "aliens who enter or attempt to enter the United States after the effective date" and to those "who must seek admission … to effectuate the approval of a petition … including through consular notification, notification at a port of entry, pre-flight inspection, or pre-clearance." Lena is in the United States in F-1 status and her employer is requesting a **change of status** with a July 1, 2027 start, so no admission is being effected by the petition and she is not "currently outside the United States." **It could reach her in other circumstances:** if she instead departed and sought an H-1B visa and admission on a petition filed without the payment (consular processing, §1(b), §2(b)); if an extension of Proclamation 11069 beyond September 21, 2027 were issued and she later needed to seek H-1B admission on an unpaid petition; or conversely she could be covered by the discretionary national-interest exception in §1(c).

- **FR doc 2026-16231, "9-11 Response and Biometric Entry-Exit Fee for H-1B and L-1 Visas," 91 FR 51360–51380, final rule, published August 10, 2026, effective September 9, 2026**; docket No. USCBP-2024-0009; CBP Dec. No. 26-11; RIN 1651-AB48. **Amount:** **$4,000** per H-1B petition (**$4,500** per L-1). **Coverage:** petitions filed by "covered employers" — those with 50 or more U.S. employees and more than 50 percent of U.S. employees in H-1B or L-1 status; the rule now requires the fee on "all extension of status petitions, regardless of whether the related fraud prevention and detection fee applies," while the fee "continues to apply unchanged to petitions seeking an initial grant of status" (a change of status from F-1 to H-1B is an initial grant of H-1B status, so a covered employer would owe it). **Would it apply to Lena?** Only if her university satisfies the 50/50 test; the documents state repeatedly that "[a] petitioner is not required to pay the 9-11 Biometric Fee if they are not a covered employer" (91 FR 51366, 51367) and contain no institution-of-higher-education exclusion, so applicability turns on the employer's workforce composition, which the Federal Register does not tell us. **Status:** in force since September 9, 2026 (a final rule, not a proposal).

A cap-exempt university petition is not subject to §214(g)(1)(A), so no F-1 provision automatically extends Lena's status to July 1, 2027. ## Q9

**Answer:**
The final rule's own "Summary of Changes in the Final Rule as Compared to the NPRM" (91 FR 45096–45098) lists the changes; the pages where each is explained are given below. Five (in fact more) that affect F-1 students:

1. **Graduate-level transfers: absolute bar converted into a bar with an SEVP exception.** New **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(A)** and **(f)(8)(i)(C)–(D)**. The NPRM "proposed prohibiting an F-1 student at the graduate level from transferring, without exception"; the final rule "has amended the regulatory text to allow SEVP to authorize an exception to this transfer prohibition in extenuating circumstances" (described at 91 FR 45043 and 91 FR 45097).
2. **Same-or-lower-level bar made prospective.** New **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(C)**. It now applies only to aliens "who have completed a program after September 15, 2026" — a change from the proposal, "clarif[ying] that this limitation of study at the same or lower educational levels applies only to programs that are completed after the effective date" (91 FR 45038; 91 FR 45097).
3. **Time limit and notice requirement on DHS's power to delay the transfer/objective limits.** New **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(E)**: DHS may delay or suspend paragraphs (f)(5)(ii)(A)–(C) only "[u]ntil September 14, 2028," and must announce any delay/suspension by Federal Register notice plus the SEVP website (adding the FR notice requirement was new in the final rule) (91 FR 45097).
4. **Latest permissible post-completion OPT start date shortened from 60 to 30 days after the program end date.** **8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(i)(D)** — the final rule replaced "60" with "30," "align[ing] with the 30-day period that was proposed in the NPRM under 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(i)(B)(2) and with the 30-day period of preparation for departure" (91 FR 45096–45097; discussion at 91 FR 45046).
5. **Transfer procedure and "first academic year" conditions rewritten.** New **8 CFR 214.2(f)(8)(i)(D)** adds the word "first" (first academic year completed at the school that issued the initial I-20); **8 CFR 214.2(f)(8)(i)(H)** substitutes "begin or resume classes" for "resume classes"; and **8 CFR 214.2(f)(8)(ii)** was revised to "clarify the previously proposed transfer procedure language" (91 FR 45097).

Three more changes that directly affect F-1 students, in case a sixth is wanted:
6. **Early program completion / departure clarified.** New **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(v)** now states expressly that if the student ends study or training before the period of admission expires, the student (and dependents) must, within 30 days of the end date, depart or seek to maintain lawful status — and that a student who fails to maintain a full course of study gets no departure period at all (91 FR 45096; discussion at 91 FR 45016).
7. **Post-completion OPT extension-of-stay route clarified.** New **8 CFR 214.2(f)(10)(ii)(D)**: "Unless described in Sec. 214.1(m)(1)(i)," a student recommended for post-completion OPT must apply for employment authorization "and either apply for an extension of stay with USCIS or seek admission through CBP after travel abroad" (91 FR 45097).
8. **Transition-paragraph structure for the OPT Form I-539 exemption.** New **8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(ii)–(iii)**: DHS "reserves the discretion to extend the period exempting the filing of the Form I-539 … beyond March 18, 2027, in 6-month increments by publication of a notification in the Federal Register" — moved into a standalone paragraph "to correctly reflect that the new paragraph (iii) applies for the entire subsection" (91 FR 45096).

(Also listed in the same Summary of Changes but not F-1-specific: removal of the NPRM's proposed 8 CFR 214.1(c)(5) language; the public-high-school charter-school clarification at (f)(5)(i)(C); title changes at (f)(5)(ii) and (f)(8); the J-1 changes; and new 8 CFR 248.1(e).)

FR doc 2026-14439: Summary of Changes at 91 FR 45096–45098; underlying discussions at 91 FR 45038 (same/lower-level prospective), 45043 (graduate transfer exception), 45046 (60→30 days), 45016 (early completion), 45097 (paragraph-by-paragraph list). Regulatory text at 91 FR 45124–45127 and 45123.

The "Summary of Changes" is DHS's own characterization; where the preamble and the codified text diverge, the regulatory text controls. ## Q11

**Answer:**
**What the final rule actually says (and does not say).**

**Cost.** The final rule does **not** set the dollar amount of the extension-of-stay filing fee. The codified text requires only that the student remit "the appropriate fee" with the form (8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(A), 91 FR 45126; same for dependents, 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iv), 91 FR 45126). The preamble says the "revenue raised by USCIS through the Form I-539 … filing fee is intended to cover the cost of processing and adjudicating EOS and change of status requests" (91 FR 45015), and DHS repeatedly notes that "USCIS is a fee-funded agency and established fees for the EOS applications to support the workload" (91 FR 45083) and "may set fees to support the additional workload" (91 FR 45031). The only dollar figures in the document are: (i) **commenter** statements — "a $420 fee, potential biometrics" (91 FR 45055) and "$555 per application including biometrics" (91 FR 45065); and (ii) **DHS's own cost estimates** — an average of **$490** for legal help, applied to 24.5% of expected EOS filers (91 FR 45083); PRA burden of **1.667 hours** per paper I-539, **1 hour** per e-filed I-539, **0.35 hours** per I-539A supplement, and **1.17 hours** for biometrics (91 FR 45120); and annualized EOS costs to nonimmigrants of **$317.9 million to $317.3 million** (3% and 7% discount rates) (91 FR 45116).

**Processing time.** The rule sets **no decision deadline and no service standard**. DHS "declines" the commenters' request for "service standards and metrics, including target processing times … and backlog dashboards" (91 FR 45015); it "cannot guarantee processing times for applications filed at USCIS due to numerous governing factors" (91 FR 45025); and it will only "continue to explore expanding premium processing for Form I-539 for affected populations requesting an EOS" (91 FR 45023). Commenters' figures, which are not DHS findings, include "around 3.5 months" (91 FR 44999), "processing times for I-539s often exceed 240 days" and up to 12–18 months (91 FR 45031, 45036), and "up to 18 months" (91 FR 45048). The one DHS processing-time datum is about EADs, not I-539s: "USCIS's average EAD processing time is typically 60-120 days for foreign students" (91 FR 45032), offered as the reason a 240-day employment extension suffices.

**Suggested handout sentences (accuracy-checked against the above):**
"The 2026 fixed-admission rule does not set the Form I-539 fee or any deadline for USCIS to decide an extension of stay; you pay whatever fee USCIS's fee schedule requires when you file, and DHS says only that it 'cannot guarantee processing times.' File early — DHS encourages filing within the six months before your authorized stay expires — because an extension application received after your program end date keeps you in status while it is pending but, under 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii), you may not continue on-campus or CPT employment until it is approved."

**Basis:**
FR doc 2026-14439: 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(A), (f)(7)(iv) at 91 FR 45126; 91 FR 45015 (fee funds adjudication; DHS declines service standards), 45023 (premium processing), 45025 (cannot guarantee processing times), 45031 (fees; commenter processing times), 45032 (EAD 60–120 days), 45036 and 45048 (commenter processing times), 45055 and 45065 (commenter fee figures), 45083 ($490 legal-help average; fee-funded), 45110 (DHS encourages filing within six months), 45116 (annualized costs), 45120 (PRA hour burdens).

**Uncertainty:**
Because the fee is set outside this rulemaking, the rule cannot tell the adviser the current dollar amount; and because the rule fixes no adjudication deadline, any processing-time statement in a handout can only describe DHS's stated inability to guarantee times or repeat commenters' reports. Any figure quoted must be attributed.

## Q12

**Answer:**
**(a) Yes — an I-539 received during the 60 days after her I-20 program end date is timely.** For a D/S transition student, the "authorized period of stay" runs to the program end date **plus the 60-day departure period** (8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)), i.e., May 15, 2027 + 60 = **July 14, 2027**. **8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B)** then provides that an extension application "is considered timely filed if the receipt date … is on or before the date the authorized period of stay expires, which includes the … period provided in paragraph (f)(5)(v)," and expressly that "[n]otwithstanding Sec. 214.1(c)(4), USCIS must receive the extension of stay application on or before the expiration of the previously authorized period of stay." Inside the 60 days, she is still within her authorized period of stay, so receipt by July 14, 2027 is timely. Filing after July 14, 2027 is not.

**(b) No — she does not keep the automatic extension of on-campus or CPT employment.** Two provisions control. First, **8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)** limits the transition authorization for work: "any authorized employment or training continues until the program end date on such F or J nonimmigrant's Form I-20 ... as endorsed by the designated school official ... or expiration date on the alien's ... EAD" — i.e., to **May 15, 2027**, not through the 60 days. Second, **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii)** provides that "[i]f an F-1 student files an extension of stay application during the 30-day period provided in paragraph (f)(5)(v) of this section, he or she does not receive an automatic extension of authorized employment, including on-campus, CPT, and severe economic hardship, and must wait for approval of the extension of stay application (and employment authorization application, if required) before engaging in CPT or employment" (repeated at 91 FR 45106 n.325, 45107 nn.328 and 332, and 45110). A student who has finished her degree program also has no continuing basis for on-campus employment, which is tied to pursuing a full course of study. So she remains in status and may study, but any on-campus or CPT work stops at the program end date and cannot resume until the extension is approved.

**Recommendation for the adviser:** Have Priya file the Form I-539 well before her program end date rather than during the 60 days — DHS encourages filing "within the six months preceding the expiration of their stay" (91 FR 45110), and footnote 338 confirms "there is no prohibition on filing the form before a certain date ahead of expiration." A pre-May 15, 2027 filing is unquestionably timely, avoids any argument about the 60-day window in (m)(1) versus the 30-day window named in (f)(7)(iii)(B), and puts her in the (f)(5)(viii) posture for any authorized employment during the pendency. Advise her in writing that filing during the 60 days is timely but produces no work authorization.

**Basis:**
8 CFR 214.1(m)(1) at 91 FR 45123; 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii) and (f)(7)(iii)(B) at 91 FR 45126; preamble at 91 FR 45106 n.325, 45107 nn.328/332, 45110 & n.338. FR doc 2026-14439.

**Uncertainty:**
8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B) names the "30-day period" of (f)(5)(v), while a transition student's departure period is 60 days under (m)(1); the rule does not expressly address the mismatch. My reading — that the 60-day period is part of her authorized period of stay and therefore a filing during it is timely — is the most defensible one, but a cautious adviser should not rely on it when an earlier filing is available. Also unaddressed is how the 240-day employment auto-extension measured from the I-94 date in (f)(5)(viii) applies to a student whose I-94 still reads D/S.

**Answer:**
**(a) After her January 9, 2027 reentry: authorized to remain through June 13, 2027.** Her December 19, 2026 departure ends her reliance on the D/S transition arithmetic; DHS's preamble says travel abroad during the transition "triggers conversion to the fixed-date regime. ## Q14

**Answer:**
**(a) The document.** **FR doc 2026-20660, "Optional Practical Training Fees," 91 FR 64566–64600 — a notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM)** published **October 8, 2026**; agency **Department of Homeland Security (U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement)**; docket **DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100**; RIN **1653-AB01**; CFR affected: **8 CFR 214**. **Status:** proposal only — no final rule and no effective date. Deadlines it sets: written **comments due November 9, 2026**; comments on the information collection due **December 7, 2026** (91 FR 64566); and, as proposed, the rule would **take effect 60 days after publication of the final rule** (proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(3)), with the fees applying to DSO recommendations **dated on or after** that effective date.

**(b) The $30,000 amount — with a textual caveat.** Proposed **8 CFR 214.13(i)(2)** (91 FR 64600) requires a school to pay **$30,000** "prior to a subsequent recommendation of the alien to participate in OPT … if the alien has previously participated in OPT **and paid the initial OPT fee of $70,000**," and the preamble states the $30,000 "would apply to any type of OPT that an F-1 student participates in after having completed their initial OPT (regardless of whether it is another pre-completion OPT, post-completion OPT, or **STEM OPT extension**)" (91 FR 64577). A 24-month STEM OPT extension is a subsequent OPT recommendation, so **$30,000**, not $70,000. The caveat: the text conditions the $30,000 on the student having previously **paid** the $70,000, and Daniel's initial post-completion OPT was recommended in 2026, before any fee existed. The proposal does not say what happens to students whose first OPT predates the fee; the two available readings are $30,000 (because it is a "subsequent" recommendation) or no fee (because the $30,000 clause presupposes a prior $70,000 payment and the $70,000 clause applies only to the "first time" a student is recommended, which has already occurred).

**(c) Who pays, when, what follows non-payment, refunds.** The **SEVP-certified school**, not the student, pays (§II.C and proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i); 91 FR 64577). **When:** "prior to the DSO recommending a student for OPT" — the DSO "must confirm that the school has paid the applicable OPT fee for the student … and then update SEVIS with the OPT fee payment information" before issuing the recommendation (proposed 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(ii); 91 FR 64577). **If not paid:** the DSO may not enter the recommendation, and "USCIS would not grant employment authorization to any student where the school has failed to pay the applicable OPT fee prior to issuing an OPT recommendation" (proposed 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(iii); 91 FR 64577). **Refundable? Only conditionally:** the school may request a refund if the student "has not received an employment authorization document" for the OPT (or OPT extension) associated with the fee; the DSO must first remove the recommendation in SEVIS; SEVP decides case by case; and the fee "will not be refunded under any circumstances once the F-1 student has received an employment authorization document" — refund determinations are "final and not … appealable" (proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1)–(2); 91 FR 64577, 64600).

**(d) When the fee would apply, and whether timing helps Daniel.** Proposed **8 CFR 214.13(i)(3)** applies the $70,000 to "each alien who receives a DSO recommendation for OPT that is dated on or after [60 days after date of publication of the final rule]" (91 FR 64600), with the $30,000 applying to later subsequent recommendations. So the trigger is the **date of the DSO's recommendation**, not the I-765 filing date or the EAD start date. **Yes, one timing lever exists:** if the DSO's STEM OPT recommendation is **dated before the effective date**, the fee would not apply under the proposed transition rule. Because his DSO "expects to recommend … in April 2027," whether he is inside the rule depends entirely on when the final rule is published plus 60 days — if publication plus 60 days falls before the April 2027 recommendation date, he is caught. (The proposal would not, as drafted, take account of his having begun OPT before the fee existed.)

**(e) Under the rules in force today.** Daniel is a D/S transition student who has not departed, so **8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)** authorizes him to remain until the later of his EAD expiry (June 30, 2027) or his I-20 program end date, capped at November 14, 2030, "plus the departure period of 60 days": June 30, 2027 + 60 days = 31 (July) + 29 (August) = **August 29, 2027**. For the STEM OPT period he must file **Form I-765** — and, because he would file on **April 12, 2027**, which is **after March 18, 2027**, he is **not** within the Form I-539 exemption of **8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(i)** and must also file a **Form I-539** for an extension of stay (8 CFR 214.1(m)(1) last sentence; 8 CFR 214.2(f)(10)(ii)(D)), unless DHS extends the exemption under 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(iii). **Work authorization while pending:** 8 CFR 274a.12(b)(6)(iv), which the final rule left unchanged, continues his post-completion OPT EAD for up to **180 days** after it expires — June 30, 2027 + 180 days = 31 (July) + 31 (August) + 30 (September) + 31 (October) + 30 (November) + 27 (December) = approximately **December 27, 2027** (see 91 FR 45002, 45024, 45037, 45101). **If approved:** a 24-month STEM OPT extension measured from July 1, 2027 (the proposal itself describes the "24-month OPT extension under paragraph (f)(10)(ii)(C)," 91 FR 64599) runs to **June 30, 2029**, and as a transition student he may remain until the EAD expiration plus 60 days: June 30, 2029 + 60 days = **August 29, 2029** (8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(i)).

**Basis:**
FR doc 2026-20660: 91 FR 64566 (summary, docket, RIN, comment dates), 64576–64577 (§V.A, the two amounts, who pays, when, non-payment, refunds, transition and effective date), 64599–64600 (proposed 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(ii)–(iii) and 214.13(i)(1)–(3)). Under current rules: FR doc 2026-14439 — 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1) and (m)(1)(i) at 91 FR 45123; 8 CFR 214.2(f)(10)(ii)(D) at 91 FR 45127; and the preamble at 91 FR 45002, 45024, 45037, 45101 (8 CFR 274a.12(b)(6)(iv) 180-day auto-extension unchanged).

**Uncertainty:**
Three gaps: (i) the proposal does not resolve the case of students whose first OPT predates the fee, so $30,000 versus $0 for Daniel is a textual question I cannot close from these documents; (ii) the 24-month STEM OPT duration comes from the rule's cross-references to 8 CFR 214.2(f)(10)(ii)(C) rather than from regulatory text reprinted in the Federal Register excerpts I read, so the June 30, 2029 date assumes a full 24-month grant; and (iii) whether DHS will extend the March 18, 2027 I-539 exemption (8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(iii)) before April 2027 is discretionary and no notice has been published.

## Q15

**Answer:**
**1. "USCIS must receive an extension-of-stay application before the program end date on the student's I-20." — Partly correct.** The *timeliness* deadline is later: **8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B)** makes an application timely if USCIS receives it "on or before the expiration of the authorized period of stay, including the 30-day period provided in paragraph (f)(5)(v)," i.e., by the I-94 admit-until date (program end + 30). But the program end date is the operative deadline for **employment**: **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii)** says a student who files "during the 30-day period" gets no automatic extension of on-campus, CPT, or severe economic hardship employment. **Reword:** "To keep working without interruption, USCIS must receive your extension application by your program end date. To be timely at all, USCIS must receive it by the end date on your I-94 — your program end date plus 30 days — but if you file in that 30-day window you cannot work while it is pending. DHS encourages filing within the six months before your stay expires (91 FR 45110)."

**2. "The four-year maximum period of admission is counted from the day the student enters the United States." — Incorrect.** Under **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i)** the maximum runs from the program start date, and both the 30 pre-start days and the 30 departure days "do not count toward the maximum length of stay." The preamble is explicit: "the calculation of the 4-year maximum periods of admission would not begin from the date of admission during the initial 30-day window, but from the program start date" (91 FR 45015–45016; see also 91 FR 45016 §E.2). **Reword:** "The four-year maximum is counted from your program start date, not your entry date; the 30 days you may arrive early and the 30 days you may stay afterward do not count."

**3. "If USCIS has still not decided a timely filed extension application 240 days after the I-94 date, the student may stay and keep studying but must stop any on-campus job." — Essentially correct.** **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii)** gives authorized stay "until USCIS issues a decision on the extension of stay application" with no 240-day outer limit, and extends on-campus/CPT/severe-economic-hardship employment only "for up to 240 days beginning from the end date of his or her period of admission as indicated on the … Form I-94." So study continues; employment stops at day 240. Two refinements: the auto-extension covers only those three employment types, and (unlike J-1, 8 CFR 214.2(j)(1)(vii)(A), which requires a subsequent extension request to remain past 240 days) the F-1 text imposes no such additional filing. **Reword:** "You may stay and study as long as the application is pending, but work authorization expires 240 days after your I-94 date unless USCIS approves sooner."

**4. "A student in an English language training program who falls seriously ill can extend beyond 24 months on medical grounds." — Incorrect as stated.** **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i)(A)** caps an ELT student's "maximum of admission period of 24 months, plus an additional 30-day period," and the preamble describes this as "an aggregate limit for F-1 students to participate in a language training program" including breaks and vacation, retained in the final rule as an anti-abuse measure (91 FR 45103; 91 FR 45013). The illness ground in **8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(i)(C)(2)(ii)** exists, but the length of any extension is bounded: the preamble states the grant may be "up to the period of time needed to complete the program … not to exceed 4 years, unless the alien is a border commuter, enrolled in language training, or attending a public high school" (91 FR 45110) — i.e., the ELT cap is the ceiling, not 4 years. The documents do not create a medical exception to the 24-month ELT limit. **Reword:** "Language-training students are limited to 24 months of language study; a documented illness or compelling academic reason can support an extension of stay, but the rule does not create a medical exception to the 24-month cap."

**5. "A degree program accredited as a five-year program has to be shortened, or issued on two I-20s, to fit the four-year limit." — Incorrect.** DHS addressed this directly: "The commenters are mistaken when they think that accredited programs will need to be shortened to fit the 4-year admission period. That is untrue. If the program has been accredited as a 5-year program, the I-20 … will state the full program length. The student will need to apply for an EOS with USCIS prior to the expiration of his or her currently authorized period of stay using the same I-20 … and may continue to study while the application is pending. If the student has not committed any crimes or otherwise violated his or her status, then the EOS should be granted and the program of study completed as accredited" (91 FR 45039–45040; accord 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(i)(C)(1), (f)(7)(vi)). **Reword:** "A five-year accredited program stays on one I-20 at its full length; you are admitted for four years and must file one extension of stay for the remainder."

**6. "A student who travels abroad and is readmitted on an I-20 with a later program end date gets a new admission period from CBP, and then does not need an extension of stay from USCIS for that time." — Mostly correct, with two qualifications.** DHS allows exactly this: it "has opted to provide flexibility by allowing F and J nonimmigrants to either file for an EOS or depart and reenter the United States to extend their stay … the decision is up to the individual" (91 FR 45025), and **8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(i)(B)** provides that an alien who seeks admission "with a Form I-20 for a program end date beyond their previously authorized period of admission … may be admitted for the period specified in Sec. 214.2(f)(5), subject to the requirements in paragraph (c)(8)." Qualifications: (i) the new admission is capped at 4 years or program length, whichever is shorter, plus 30 days (8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(i)(A)); and (ii) if an extension application is pending, reentry on the later-dated I-20 may cause it to be deemed abandoned (8 CFR 214.1(c)(8)(ii)), so the two routes are alternatives, not cumulative. **Reword:** "You can generally extend your stay either by filing an extension with USCIS or by departing and being readmitted on an I-20 with a later program end date — but the admission is capped at four years or your program length, and if you have an extension pending, reentering on a later-dated I-20 may abandon it. Discuss the choice with your adviser before traveling."

**7. "The exemption from filing Form I-539 for OPT applicants covers I-765s filed within six months of the rule's effective date, so the last filing day is March 15, 2027." — Incorrect on the date and on the framing.** **8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(i)** exempts an F-1 recommended for post-completion OPT who files the I-765 "before his or her period of admission expires, including the 60 day departure period, … on or before **March 18, 2027**" (and, for STEM OPT, before the current EAD expires, also on or before March 18, 2027). The date is **March 18, 2027**, not March 15, 2027, and the exemption is not defined as "within six months of the effective date" but as a fixed filing deadline, which DHS may extend "in 6-month increments by publication of a notification in the Federal Register" (8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(iii)). **Reword:** "If you file your OPT (or STEM OPT) I-765 on or before March 18, 2027 and before your authorized stay (including the 60-day departure period) expires, you do not need a separate Form I-539 for the OPT period; DHS may extend that date in six-month increments by Federal Register notice."

**Where the text and the preamble diverge:** on statement 1, the codified timeliness rule (8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B)) permits filing through the 30-day departure period while 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii) and its preamble notes (91 FR 45106 n.325, 45107 nn.328/332, 45110) attach the employment penalty to the same window — the regulatory text controls, and the two provisions are consistent only if read as a filing deadline plus a work-authorization consequence. On statement 4, the codified ELT cap in 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i)(A) does not itself say extensions are subject to it, whereas the preamble's description of extension length (91 FR 45110) treats ELT as outside the 4-year extension ceiling; the codified cap in (f)(5)(i)(A) controls, supported by the preamble. On statement 6, the codified "may be admitted" (8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(i)(B)) is discretionary, while the preamble's "either file for an EOS or depart and reenter" reads as a freestanding option; the regulation controls, so readmission is not guaranteed.

**Basis:**
8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(i)(A)–(B), (c)(8)(ii) at 91 FR 45122–45123; 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(i), (m)(1)(iii) at 91 FR 45123; 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i), (f)(5)(i)(A), (f)(5)(v), (f)(5)(viii), (f)(7)(i)(C)(1)–(2), (f)(7)(iii)(B), (f)(7)(vi), (f)(11)(i)(D) at 91 FR 45124–45127; 8 CFR 214.2(j)(1)(vii)(A) at 91 FR 45130. Preamble: 91 FR 45015–45016 (calculation from program start), 45039–45040 & n.197 (five-year accredited programs; earliest filing date), 45013 & 45103 (ELT 24-month cap), 45025 (EOS or travel), 45106 n.325, 45107 nn.328/332, 45110 (timeliness, 30-day-window employment bar, six-month encouragement, extension ceilings), 45024 (OPT needs both approvals). FR doc 2026-14439.

**Uncertainty:**
Statements 3 and 6 depend on provisions whose operative effect is partly discretionary ("may be admitted") or measured from a date the rule defines only indirectly ("the end date of his or her period of admission as indicated on the … Form I-94"); and the ELT/illness point is answered by negative implication from the preamble rather than by an express regulatory sentence saying illness cannot extend beyond 24 months.

## Q16

**Answer:**
**(a) Lin's I-94 admit-until date: September 21, 2031.** **8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(i)(A)** admits an F-1 for "a maximum period of 4 years or the length of program as specified on Form I-20, whichever is shorter, plus additional 30 day periods for arrival and departure as provided in Sec. 214.2(f)(5)(i)." The program (May 14, 2033) is longer than four years, so the four-year cap governs, and it is counted from the **program start date**, not the entry date (8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i); preamble, 91 FR 45015–45016). Arithmetic: program start **August 23, 2027** + 4 years = the four-year period ends **August 22, 2031**; + 30 days = 9 days left in August + 21 in September = **September 21, 2031**. (Her August 2, 2027 entry is inside the 30-day early-arrival window and does not count toward the four years.)

**(b) To stay past September 21, 2031 she must file a Form I-539 extension of stay.** **What she submits** — **8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(A)**: the USCIS form with "the updated, properly endorsed Form I-20 …, submitting evidence of sufficient funds to cover expenses; appearing for any biometrics collection required by 8 CFR 103.16; and remitting the appropriate fee"; **8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(ii)** requires the I-20 to be endorsed with the DSO's recommendation and new program end date. **On what ground** — **8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(i)**: she must have maintained status (A), be pursuing a full course of study (B), and have either "[a] currently issued Form I-20 … indicating additional time is left to complete his or her program of study" ((C)(1)) — which her I-20 already shows, since May 14, 2033 is beyond the four-year admission — or documentation of a compelling academic reason, documented illness, or circumstances beyond her control ((C)(2)). DHS confirms the same I-20 used to enter suffices: the student applies "using the same I-20 … used to enter the country and may continue to study while the application is pending," and "the EOS should be granted" absent violations (91 FR 45039–45040). **How early** — **no earliest date**: "With respect to the earliest filing date for a Form I-539, there is no prohibition on filing the form before a certain date ahead of expiration" (91 FR 45039 n.197; 91 FR 45110 n.338), and DHS encourages filing "within the six months preceding the expiration of their stay" (91 FR 45110). Practically: any time, sensibly from about March 2031; and to preserve any employment auto-extension, before the end of her authorized employment period (8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii)), since 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B) requires receipt on or before the expiration of the authorized period of stay, including the 30-day period. **If granted in full** — **8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(vi)**: an extension "for the period of time necessary to complete the program as listed on the F-1 student's Form I-20 … not to exceed 4 years," with the 30 departure days not counting against the maximum; so to the program end date **May 14, 2033**, plus 30 days = 17 days left in May + 13 in June = **June 13, 2033**.

**(c) The 2029 master's does not impair her PhD.** The same-or-lower-level bar, **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(C)**, applies to an alien who has "completed a program … at one educational level" and then seeks F-1 status "through a program at the same educational level or a lower educational level." A master's awarded en route within her PhD is not a new program of study at a lower level that she "begins"; she continues the same doctoral program, and upward progression is expressly status-preserving under **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(B)**. She is also not "changing educational objectives" (major or level) under **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(A)**, which for graduate students bars changes "at any point during their program of study." The DSO should ensure the SEVIS record and I-20 continue to reflect the doctoral program (and the rule's NCES-based level taxonomy, discussed at 91 FR 45038 and 45093), so the intermediate award is not recorded as a new program.

**(d) The August 2030 trip: highly likely a new, full fixed admission period — and then the (b) filing would not be needed; but certainty is limited.** Readmission is governed by **8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(i)(A)**: with a program end date of May 14, 2033, the remaining program (about 2.8 years from August 2030) is shorter than four years, so she "may be admitted" for the program length plus a 30-day departure period, i.e., to May 14, 2033 + 30 days = **June 13, 2033** — the same date an approved extension in (b) would give her, which would make a separate extension unnecessary during that period. DHS describes travel as converting a D/S student to the fixed-date regime and issuing "a new I-94 with a date certain" (91 FR 45017–45018), and it treats departure-and-reentry as an alternative to filing an EOS (91 FR 45025). The uncertainties are real: the regulation says "may be admitted" (CBP discretion), the admission cannot be assumed to exceed four years or the program length, and the preamble's travel-as-alternative discussion does not address readmission where the traveler has no more than four years of program left. An adviser should not treat this as a certainty and should confirm the I-94 on return.

**(e) Her husband.** **Until when he may stay:** only as long as Lin. **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i)(E)** provides that "[t]he authorized period of stay for F-2 dependents may not exceed the authorized period of stay of the principal F-1 student," and the preamble states that if the principal's stay is shortened "then the dependents must depart at the same time as the principal even if their I-94 has a longer period of stay" (91 FR 45016). A later I-94 date on his record therefore does not extend him beyond **September 21, 2031** (or whatever date Lin is ultimately admitted to). **How he is covered when Lin applies:** **8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iv)** requires an F-2 spouse seeking to accompany her during the additional period either to "be included on the principal F-1 student's application for an extension of stay or file their own extension of stay application," submitting the endorsed I-20, funds evidence, biometrics, and the fee, and demonstrating the qualifying relationship, maintenance of status, and no unauthorized employment; extensions for F-2s "may not exceed the authorized admission period of the principal." **The fee:** the preamble states that dependents "may be included in the principal's EOS application for no additional fee if statuses expire simultaneously. If filed separately, each requires a fee" (91 FR 45029), and that where the dependent "files a Form I-539A as part of the primary applicant's EOS request on a Form I-539, only one fee will be required" (91 FR 45110). Since their statuses expire on the same date (his I-94 cannot lawfully extend beyond hers), including him on her application with a Form I-539A is the single-fee route; filing separately means a second fee.

**Basis:**
8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(i)(A) at 91 FR 45122; 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i), (f)(5)(i)(A), (f)(5)(i)(E), (f)(5)(ii)(A)–(C), (f)(5)(viii), (f)(7)(i)(A)–(C), (f)(7)(ii), (f)(7)(iii)(A)–(B), (f)(7)(iv), (f)(7)(vi) at 91 FR 45124–45127; 8 CFR 214.3 not implicated. Preamble: 91 FR 45015–45016 (four years from program start; F-2 cannot outlast principal), 45016 (dependent must depart with principal), 45017–45018 (travel converts to fixed date; new I-94 with date certain), 45025 (EOS or depart-and-reenter), 45029 (dependents no additional fee if included and statuses expire together), 45038 and 45093 (educational levels/upward progression), 45039–45040 and nn.197 (five-year programs; same I-20; no earliest filing date), 45110 and n.338 (six-month encouragement; no earliest date; F-2 fees; extension ceiling), 45106 n.325 and 45107 n.328 (employment bar if filed in the 30-day window). FR doc 2026-14439.

**Uncertainty:**
The rule does not specify inclusive/exclusive counting for the 4-year period, so the 2031 date could be argued as September 22, 2031 if the program start day is counted as day one; I used the rule's own convention of counting the four years from the program start date to August 22, 2031 and adding 30 days. In (d), 8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(i)(A) says "may be admitted," so a full re-admission for the remaining program length is the expected but not guaranteed outcome, and the rule does not address whether an earlier EOS remains necessary or whether a readmission super-sedes it. In (e), the "no additional fee" statement appears in a preamble response to comments (91 FR 45029) and in the instructions discussion at 91 FR 45110 rather than in the codified text, which says only "remitting the appropriate fee" (8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iv)); the codified text should be treated as controlling if there is a conflict.
</submission>

Abstract:
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) is amending the regulations concerning the 9-11 Response and Biometric Entry-Exit Fee for certain H-1B and L-1 Visas (9-11 Biometric Fee). The regulatory changes correct DHS's interpretation of statutory language to require that covered employers submit the 9-11 Biometric Fee for all extension of status petitions, regardless of whether the related fraud prevention and detection fee applies, which includes extension of status petitions that do not involve a change of employer. The 9-11 Biometric Fee continues to apply unchanged to petitions seeking an initial grant of status. The changes also help DHS comply with its congressional mandate to implement a biometric entry-exit system.

tools.name: fr_search

query.description: Full-text search terms; "" for none. Supports quoted phrases, e.g. "\"extension of stay\" F-1".
query.title: Query

doc_type.description: Document types: RULE, PRORULE (proposed rule), NOTICE, PRESDOCU (presidential document). null for all.
doc_type.title: Doc Type

agency.description: Agency slugs, e.g. homeland-security-department, u-s-citizenship-and-immigration-services, u-s-immigration-and-customs-enforcement, state-department, labor-department, executive-office-of-the-president.
agency.title: Agency

pres_type.description: Presidential document subtypes (use with doc_type PRESDOCU).
pres_type.title: Pres Type

cfr.description: CFR title:part affected, e.g. 8:214. The part must be numeric; lettered parts are not supported by this filter.
cfr.title: Cfr

tools.description: Search U.S. Federal Register documents (rules, proposed rules, notices, presidential documents) by keywords and filters. Prints document numbers, titles, types, dates, citations, dockets, RINs and abstracts.

tools.name: fr_doc
tools.description: Metadata for one Federal Register document: title, type, action, citation, page range, publication/signing/effective dates, comment deadline, docket, RIN, CFR parts affected, corrections, abstract.

tools.name: fr_toc
tools.description: Outline of a document's full text: headings with line numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_grep

pattern.description: Python regular expression, searched over the whole text (a match may span lines). ^ and $ match at line boundaries; . does not match a newline.
pattern.title: Pattern

context.description: Lines of context around each match (default 2, at most 10).
context.title: Context

tools.description: Regex search inside one document's full text. Shows the lines of each match with line numbers, context lines and the FR page of each match. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_text
tools.description: Read a document's full text by line range, with line numbers. [[Page N]] markers give FR page numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

rationale.description: Brief evidence: what the submission says (quote or locate it) and any tool checks. Explain any 'unclear'.
rationale.title: Rationale

rubric_feedback.description: Problems with the rubric or answer key that this submission exposed (wrong expected answers, ambiguous criteria, valid answers the key misses). Empty string if none.
rubric_feedback.title: Rubric Feedback

tools.name: fr_search

query.description: Full-text search terms; "" for none. Supports quoted phrases, e.g. "\"extension of stay\" F-1".
query.title: Query

doc_type.description: Document types: RULE, PRORULE (proposed rule), NOTICE, PRESDOCU (presidential document). null for all.
doc_type.title: Doc Type

agency.description: Agency slugs, e.g. homeland-security-department, u-s-citizenship-and-immigration-services, u-s-immigration-and-customs-enforcement, state-department, labor-department, executive-office-of-the-president.
agency.title: Agency

pres_type.description: Presidential document subtypes (use with doc_type PRESDOCU).
pres_type.title: Pres Type

cfr.description: CFR title:part affected, e.g. 8:214. The part must be numeric; lettered parts are not supported by this filter.
cfr.title: Cfr

tools.description: Search U.S. Federal Register documents (rules, proposed rules, notices, presidential documents) by keywords and filters. Prints document numbers, titles, types, dates, citations, dockets, RINs and abstracts.

tools.name: fr_doc
tools.description: Metadata for one Federal Register document: title, type, action, citation, page range, publication/signing/effective dates, comment deadline, docket, RIN, CFR parts affected, corrections, abstract.

tools.name: fr_toc
tools.description: Outline of a document's full text: headings with line numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_grep

pattern.description: Python regular expression, searched over the whole text (a match may span lines). ^ and $ match at line boundaries; . does not match a newline.
pattern.title: Pattern

context.description: Lines of context around each match (default 2, at most 10).
context.title: Context

tools.description: Regex search inside one document's full text. Shows the lines of each match with line numbers, context lines and the FR page of each match. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_text
tools.description: Read a document's full text by line range, with line numbers. [[Page N]] markers give FR page numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

rationale.description: Brief evidence: what the submission says (quote or locate it) and any tool checks. Explain any 'unclear'.
